it-2006-cs-1.approach: Apply the total probability theorem over the two equally likely temperature cases and solve for the unknown conditional probability.

steps.title: Set up total probability
steps.body:
Let $H$ = temperature above $25^\circ$C, $L$ = at/below. $P(H)=P(L)=0.5$, $P(R\mid L)=0.4$, $P(R)=0.6$.

$$P(R)=P(R\mid L)P(L)+P(R\mid H)P(H)$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 0.4 is the probability for the cooler case, not the warmer one.
This is the overall probability $P(R)$, not the conditional one.

pitfalls: Forgetting to weight each case by $0.5$.

it-2006-cs-2.approach: For each operation look for a $z$ with $f(a,z)=a=f(z,a)$ for every $a$; a single counterexample kills a candidate.

steps.title: f(x,y) = x + y − 3
steps.body: $f(a,z)=a+z-3=a \iff z=3$, and $f(3,a)=3+a-3=a$. Since $3\in N$, **$z=3$ is an identity**.

steps.title: f(x,y) = max(x,y)
steps.body: Take $z$ = the least natural number (1, or 0 if $0\in N$). Then $\max(a,z)=a=\max(z,a)$ for all $a$. **Identity exists.**

steps.title: f(x,y) = x^y
steps.body:
Right identity needs $a^z=a$ for all $a$, forcing $z=1$. But $f(1,a)=1^a=1\neq a$ for $a=2$. So no two-sided identity.

Hence operations **1 and 2** only.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: 3 is the identity for 1, the least natural number for 2.
Exponentiation has only a right identity (1), not a left one.
Exponentiation fails, and max does have an identity.

pitfalls: Accepting $z=1$ for $x^y$ after checking only one side: $1^a=1$.

it-2006-cs-3.approach: Trace each string through the DFA. Observing that $a$ toggles s/r and $b$ toggles s/t makes the trace mechanical.

steps.title: Trace u = abbaba
steps.body: $s\xrightarrow{a}r\xrightarrow{b}r\xrightarrow{b}r\xrightarrow{a}s\xrightarrow{b}t\xrightarrow{a}t$. Ends in $t$ (final) — **accepted**.

scene.caption: u = abbaba ends in t: accept

steps.title: Trace v = bab
steps.body: $s\xrightarrow{b}t\xrightarrow{a}t\xrightarrow{b}s$. Ends in $s$ — **rejected**.

scene.caption: v = bab ends in s: reject

steps.title: Trace w = aabb
steps.body:
$s\xrightarrow{a}r\xrightarrow{a}s\xrightarrow{b}t\xrightarrow{b}s$. Ends in $s$ — **rejected**.

So the automaton accepts $u$ only.

scene.caption: w = aabb ends in s: reject

answer.value: Accepts u, rejects v and w

optionAnalysis.reason: $v$ ends in $s$, so it is rejected.
Correct: only $u$ ends in the final state $t$.

pitfalls: Reading the $a$ arcs between s and r as going only one way — both directions carry $a$.
it-2006-cs-3.verification: Re-traced each string; final states t, s, s respectively.

it-2006-cs-4.approach: Every production wraps the string symmetrically (aSa, bSb) around a centre of a, b or ε, so the grammar generates exactly the palindromes over {a,b}. Pick the non-palindrome.

steps.title: Language of the grammar
steps.body: $S\to aSa\mid bSb$ adds the same symbol at both ends; $S\to a\mid b\mid\varepsilon$ gives odd/even centres. So $L(G)=\{w : w=w^R\}$.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body:
| String | Reverse | Palindrome? |
|---|---|---|
| aaaa | aaaa | yes |
| baba | abab | **no** |
| abba | abba | yes |
| babaaabab | babaaabab | yes |

So **baba** is not generated.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: baba is not a palindrome.
Odd palindrome with centre a: $bab\,a\,a\,a\,bab$ reads the same both ways.

it-2006-cs-4.verification: Derivation of babaaabab: $bSb\to baSab\to babSbab\to babaSabab\to babaaabab$.

it-2006-cs-5.approach: Read the NFA left to right: any prefix (self-loop), then a, then any one symbol, then b at the end.

steps.title: Read the path
steps.body: Start state loops on $a,b$ → $(a+b)^*$. Then $a$, then $a,b$ → $(a+b)$, then $b$ into the final state, which has no outgoing edges.

steps.title: Expression
steps.body: $$(a+b)^*\,a\,(a+b)\,b$$ — strings whose third-last symbol is $a$ and last symbol is $b$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: matches the single path through the NFA.
Excludes e.g. $baab$, which the NFA accepts.
Allows arbitrary gaps, e.g. $ab$, which the NFA rejects (needs ≥ 3 symbols).
Accepts everything, including $\varepsilon$, which the NFA rejects.

it-2006-cs-5.verification: $aab$: loop 0 times, $a$, $a$, $b$ ✓; $ab$ cannot reach the final state ✓.

it-2006-cs-6.approach: Recognise Shannon expansion: $f = x_i'f|_{x_i=0} + x_i f|_{x_i=1}$. A, B and C are valid identities; D drops the literals.

steps.title: Check A, B, C
steps.body: A and B: $x'f + xf = (x'+x)f = f$ ✓. C is the Shannon expansion on $x_n$ ✓.

steps.title: Counterexample for D
steps.body: Take $f=x_1$. Then $f(0,\ldots)+f(1,\ldots)=0+1=1$, but $f=x_1$ is $0$ when $x_1=0$. So D is **not** true in general.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct (NOT true): the cofactors are summed without $x_1'$, $x_1$; fails for $f=x_1$.

it-2006-cs-6.verification: For $f=x_1$: RHS of D is the constant 1, LHS is $x_1$.

it-2006-cs-7.approach: Add the bit patterns, then use the sign rule: overflow only when two same-sign operands give a result of opposite sign.

steps.title: Overflow?
steps.body: Operands have opposite signs, so overflow is impossible (carry into MSB = carry out = 1). Result: **0001, no overflow**.

optionAnalysis.reason: The carry-out is discarded; it is not overflow in two's complement.

pitfalls: Treating the carry-out bit as overflow.

it-2006-cs-8.approach: Bandwidth is maximised when the DMA controller keeps the bus for a whole block and the CPU services the completion interrupt fastest.

steps.title: DMA mode
steps.body: Block (burst) transfer moves the whole block in one bus grant; cycle stealing and transparent DMA move one word at a time when the bus is free, so they are slower.

steps.title: Interrupt mechanism
steps.body: Vectored interrupts jump directly to the handler; polling wastes time identifying the device. Best: **block transfer + vectored interrupts**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Transparent DMA uses only idle cycles — lowest DMA throughput; polling is slow.
Cycle stealing transfers one word per stolen cycle.

it-2006-cs-8.verification: Standard textbook ranking (Hamacher): burst > cycle stealing > transparent; vectored faster than polled.

it-2006-cs-9.approach: In any binary tree, leaves = (nodes of degree 2) + 1; degree-1 nodes do not matter.

steps.title: Count edges two ways
steps.body: Let $n_0,n_1,n_2$ be the numbers of nodes with 0, 1, 2 children. Edges $= n-1 = n_0+n_1+n_2-1$ and also $= n_1+2n_2$. Hence $n_0=n_2+1$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body: With $n_2 = 10$ internal nodes of degree 2 (and $n_1=5$ irrelevant): $$n_0 = n_2 + 1 = 10 + 1 = 11$$

optionAnalysis.reason: Adds $n_1$ to $n_2$ — degree-1 nodes do not create leaves.

it-2006-cs-10.approach: NP-complete = in NP and NP-hard. To be NP-hard it suffices that a known NP-complete problem (3-SAT) reduces to it in polynomial time.

steps.title: Direction of reduction
steps.body: If $3\text{-SAT}\le_p X$ and $X\in NP$, every NP problem reduces to 3-SAT and hence to $X$, so $X$ is NP-complete.

steps.title: Reject the others
steps.body: Reducing $X$ to 3-SAT only shows $X\in NP$. "Some problem in NP reduces to it" holds for every problem (e.g. trivial ones).

optionAnalysis.reason: Wrong direction: this holds for every NP problem.
Wrong direction; says nothing about hardness.
Too weak: any problem in P satisfies it.

it-2006-cs-10.verification: Matches the Cook–Levin based definition used by Karp reductions.

it-2006-cs-11.approach: A minimum-weight connected spanning edge set cannot contain a cycle when weights are positive, so it is a (spanning) tree.

steps.title: No cycles
steps.body: If the subset had a cycle, removing any cycle edge keeps all vertices connected and lowers the total weight (weights $>0$), contradicting minimality.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Connected + acyclic = **tree** (an MST).

optionAnalysis.reason: A Hamiltonian cycle contains a cycle; dropping an edge is cheaper.

it-2006-cs-11.verification: With zero-weight edges a cycle might survive; positivity rules that out.

it-2006-cs-12.approach: The working-set model keeps $D=\sum WSS_i$ against the frame count $m$: admit a new process when there is slack, suspend one when $D>m$.

steps.title: Working-set policy
steps.body: If $D<m$ with enough spare frames, the OS can start another process (statement 1). If $D>m$, the OS suspends a process and frees its frames (statement 2).

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both actions are part of the strategy.

it-2006-cs-12.verification: Silberschatz, Operating System Concepts, working-set model.

it-2006-cs-13.approach: Look for the Running → Ready edge. Preemption needs it (timer interrupt sends the running process back to ready); the diagram has none.

steps.title: Read the diagram
steps.body: Edges: Start→Ready, Ready→Running, Running→Terminated, Running→Blocked, Blocked→Ready. A running process leaves the CPU only by exiting or blocking.

steps.title: Judge the options
steps.body: No Running→Ready transition ⇒ scheduling cannot be preemptive. Multiprogramming and multi-user operation are possible (many processes in Ready/Blocked). So **"uses preemptive scheduling" must be FALSE**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Possible: several processes can be in Ready/Blocked.
Correct: impossible without a Running→Ready edge.
True: the CPU is released only voluntarily.
Possible: nothing in the diagram forbids multiple users.

it-2006-cs-14.approach: The natural join is on R, which is the primary key of $r_2$, so each $r_1$ tuple matches at most one $r_2$ tuple.

steps.title: Common attribute
steps.body: $r_1(P,Q,R)\bowtie r_2(R,S,T)$ joins on $R$, the key of $r_2$: each $R$ value occurs at most once in $r_2$.

steps.title: Bound
steps.body: Each of the 2000 $r_1$ tuples joins with ≤ 1 tuple, so $|r_1\bowtie r_2|\le 2000$, achieved when every $r_1.R$ appears in $r_2$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Would need some $r_1$ tuple to match several $r_2$ tuples — impossible since R is a key of $r_2$.
Sum of sizes; joins do not add.

it-2006-cs-14.verification: Example: $r_2$ holds R = 1..2500, every $r_1$ tuple has R in 1..2500 ⇒ 2000 rows.

it-2006-cs-15.approach: Codd's theorem: relational algebra, safe tuple calculus and safe domain calculus are equally expressive.

steps.title: Equivalence
steps.body: Every RA expression has an equivalent safe TRC and safe DRC expression and vice versa (Codd's theorem).

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — have the same power.

pitfalls: Unrestricted (unsafe) calculus is more expressive (can give infinite answers); safety is what makes them equal.
it-2006-cs-15.verification: Korth/Silberschatz, Database System Concepts, ch. on relational calculus.

it-2006-cs-16.approach: Cyclomatic complexity = number of linearly independent paths; a basis-path test set of that size is sufficient (never more needed) for executing every statement at least once.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: $V(G)$ counts independent paths. Testing all basis paths covers every statement and branch, so $V(G)$ tests always suffice.

steps.title: Upper bound, at least once
steps.body: Fewer tests may achieve statement coverage, so $V(G)$ is an **upper bound** on the tests needed to execute every statement **at least once**.

optionAnalysis.reason: "At most once" is not a coverage goal.
Same flaw; also not a lower bound.
Not a lower bound: statement coverage often needs fewer tests.

it-2006-cs-16.verification: Pressman, Software Engineering: "upper bound for the number of tests … executed at least once".

it-2006-cs-17.approach: Recall the McCabe formulas for a single connected component: $V(G)=E-N+2=P+1$.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: $V(G)=E-N+2p$ with $p=1$ component ⇒ $E-N+2$. Also $V(G)=P+1$ for binary predicate nodes.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: Expressions **2 and 4**.

it-2006-cs-18.approach: Recall protocol commands: HELO opens an SMTP session; PORT tells an FTP server where to open the data connection.

steps.title: HELO
steps.body: SMTP client greeting: `HELO client.example.com`.

steps.title: PORT
steps.body: FTP active-mode command giving the client IP and port for the data channel. Hence **SMTP and FTP**.

optionAnalysis.reason: HELO is not an FTP command; HTTP has no PORT command.

it-2006-cs-19.approach: Ethernet trailer has a 32-bit CRC (FCS); the IPv4 header has a 16-bit ones-complement header checksum.

steps.title: Ethernet
steps.body: Frame ends with the 4-byte Frame Check Sequence, a CRC-32.

steps.title: IPv4 header
steps.body: IPv4 header has a 16-bit header checksum (ones-complement sum), not a CRC.

optionAnalysis.reason: Ethernet uses a CRC, not a checksum.
IP does not use a CRC.

it-2006-cs-20.approach: A hash maps arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest; because the domain is larger than the range, collisions must exist.

steps.title: Statements 1 and 2
steps.body: 1 is the definition of a hash function (true). 2 reverses it (false).

steps.title: Statement 3
steps.body: Pigeonhole principle: infinitely many messages, finitely many digests ⇒ distinct messages can share a hash (true). So **1 and 3**.

it-2006-cs-20.verification: E.g. SHA-256 always outputs 256 bits regardless of input length.

it-2006-cs-21.approach: The formula says R is symmetric. Find one model where R is symmetric and one where it is not.

steps.title: Satisfiable
steps.body: Take $R=\emptyset$ (or equality): the implication holds vacuously, so the formula is satisfiable.

steps.title: Negation satisfiable
steps.body: Domain $\{1,2\}$, $R=\{(1,2)\}$: $R(1,2)$ true, $R(2,1)$ false, so the formula is false and its negation is true. Hence the formula is not valid, and both it and its negation are satisfiable.

answer.value: satisfiable and so is its negation

it-2006-cs-21.verification: Two explicit models given, one for each.

it-2006-cs-22.approach: N is geometric with success probability p; its mean is 1/p.

steps.title: Expectation via recursion
steps.body:
First toss: Head (prob $p$) ⇒ $N=1$; Tail ⇒ start over after 1 toss.
$$E=p\cdot1+(1-p)(1+E)\Rightarrow E=1+(1-p)E\Rightarrow pE=1\Rightarrow E=\frac1p$$

optionAnalysis.reason: That is the expected tosses until the first Tail.

it-2006-cs-22.verification: $p=\tfrac12$ gives $E=2$, the familiar answer for a fair coin.
